source.title: Economic impacts of AI-augmented R&D
source.authors: Tamay Besiroglu; Nicholas Emery-Xu; Neil C. Thompson

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests the compute–performance relationship on computer-vision models, extending evidence about scaling relationships beyond language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The authors cite neural scaling-law results from other work, which are not rows. Their own relevant result is the reported relationship between training compute and error on ImageNet and MS COCO. The economic production-function estimates and compute-growth estimates do not measure the power-law loss relationship and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: This is mainly an economics paper. Its main regressions estimate R&D production-function elasticities, and it builds a power law into its model (Appendix A5) rather than testing one. Its only result bearing on a claim version is Appendix I / Figure 10. That is a cross-sectional log-log association between estimated training compute and test error across published ImageNet and MS COCO models, which the authors call roughly power-law. This is weak T3 evidence for V5. The models differ in architecture, data and recipe, so compute is not varied with the other factors held fixed. No power-law exponent or comparison with other functional forms is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase over-weights the appendix. The authors' main conclusion is economic. Deep-learning computer-vision R&D is more capital-intensive than other US R&D: an optimizing firm would spend 29–44% of R&D on compute. Under a semi-endogenous growth model, widespread adoption could raise productivity growth about 1.7–2x the historical average. The roughly power-law compute–error relation (especially on ImageNet) is a side observation in Appendix I. The authors acknowledge the analysis is limited to two computer-vision tasks.
record.recipe_differences: This is an economic analysis of reported computer-vision model results, not a language-model scaling experiment; it analyzes benchmark error against estimated training compute.

fits_no_version.finding: The elasticity of proportional performance gain over a baseline model, with respect to training compute, is about 0.11–0.14 for ImageNet, about 0.25 for COCO, and 0.145–0.176 pooled (Tables 4–6). The estimates are robust to time-window length and to dropping outliers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Returns to compute in benchmark improvement over contemporaneous baselines follow a constant elasticity (an economic production-function measure, not loss scaling).

fits_no_version.finding: Human capital of the author team is positively but weakly associated with benchmark error (Figure 10 lower panels, R² 0.13–0.57). Its R&D elasticity is about 0.25–0.35.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Researcher human capital contributes to benchmark progress alongside compute.

record.problems: The evidence is limited to two computer-vision benchmarks and observational model data. The paper notes possible selection and compute-measurement errors; the compute estimates may omit trial runs and may attenuate estimated compute effects. The figure reports fit statistics, but does not establish prediction from small runs to larger runs.

untested.parts: Video and other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes. A controlled within-recipe scaling of a single model family. Whether the curve is a power law rather than another monotone form (no exponent or functional-form comparison).
Language-model pretraining loss is not measured.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Architecture effects at fixed parameter count are not tested.
No downstream-versus-scale or downstream-versus-loss analysis of language models.
No analysis of how fitting choices affect the results.

record.verdict_notes: The power-law link to scaling laws is mainly assumed: the logistic performance mapping is chosen so that it implies a power law (Appendix A5), and the paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann for it. The Figure 10 evidence is observational across heterogeneous models, so other factors (architecture, data, training recipe) vary along with compute. Selection bias and noise in the compute estimates are acknowledged. Treat any V5 support as weak.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test held-out pretraining loss of language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits are tested as predictions of substantially larger runs.
The paper does not estimate a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or compare how either grows with compute.
Architecture types occur in the dataset, but the paper does not test the effect of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Evidence is limited to ImageNet image classification and MS COCO object detection; other modalities and regimes such as video, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
The paper does not test downstream-task performance as a function of pretraining loss or language-model scale.
The paper does not test sensitivity of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations to fitting choices or setup.

rows.subject: Image classification models on ImageNet (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured model error against training compute across the dataset of models.
rows.measure: Top-1 error versus training compute; the authors describe the relationship as roughly power-law and particularly evident for ImageNet.
rows.value: R² = 0.64 and R² = 0.53 are shown in Figure 10; the extracted figure text does not identify the plotted series for each value.
rows.note: Aggregate evidence across the ImageNet models; the authors explicitly characterize the compute–error relationship as roughly power-law.
rows.check: Subject is published ImageNet models of varied architecture and recipe, not a controlled size sweep. The measure is benchmark top-1 test error, not loss. The two R² values (0.64, 0.53) most likely belong to the series split by the figure's 'Extra data No/Yes' legend; the text does not say which is which. The fit is a log-log association over roughly 4 orders of magnitude of compute, with no reported exponent. n=96 is the regression sample; the figure's sample size is not stated. 'Observed' holds only loosely: the authors' wording is 'roughly a power-law'.

rows.subject: Object detection models on MS COCO 2017 (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured model error against training compute across the dataset of models.
rows.measure: Box AP error versus training compute; the authors describe the compute–error relationship for the considered tasks as roughly power-law.
rows.note: Aggregate evidence across the object-detection models; the text says the power-law relationship is particularly evident for ImageNet.
rows.check: The fit is weak: R² = 0.38 over only about 2 orders of magnitude of compute, with error spanning roughly 50–60 Box AP error. The authors say the relation is 'particularly evident for ImageNet', which implies it is less clear here. It is cross-sectional across heterogeneous published models, and no exponent is reported.

relationships.condition: ImageNet image classification, cross-sectional across published models (about 4 orders of magnitude of compute)
relationships.reason: Error falls with training compute on a log-log plot (R² 0.64/0.53), which the authors call roughly power-law (r1). The evidence is observational and has no fitted exponent.
relationships.display_finding: Error decreased approximately as a power of training compute across published models, with log-log R² values of 0.64 and 0.53.

relationships.condition: MS COCO 2017 object detection, cross-sectional across published models (about 2 orders of magnitude of compute)
relationships.reason: The compute–error association is weak (R² = 0.38) over a narrow compute range and is less evident than for ImageNet (r2).
relationships.display_finding: The compute-error association had R² = 0.38 across approximately two orders of magnitude and was less evident than for ImageNet.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The authors report a roughly power-law relationship between compute and error, particularly evident for ImageNet (r1).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The authors report a roughly power-law compute–error relationship for the tasks studied, including object detection (r2).
